item.title: Big Read: Nobody at your lodge decided to block the AI agent. Something in your stack did.
item.description: On 18 October an AI agent working for a traveller could not see a rate at a Wyndham hotel. On 19 October it reached the guest details page. Nothing in Wyndham's published policy changed overnight, and that is the point: access to hotel inventory is now decided by bot-management software rather than by anyone's commercial judgement. item.title: Big Read: Kenya curated 75 experiences this month. Not one of them can be bought where it is displayed.
item.description: The Magical Kenya Signature Experiences collection grew to 75 entries on 15 October. The public page carries no price, no availability and no booking button, and Kenya's own draft tourism strategy already names the missing piece.

item.title: Big Read: The law that reprices every deposit your lodge takes
item.description: Treasury and the Central Bank spent the first week and a half of October taking public views on a Bill that rewrites the licensing of every company standing between a guest's card and a lodge's bank account. One of the eleven hearings was held in a hotel. The hospitality industry, which has already been taught once this year what a payment rail costs it, was largely somewhere else.

item.title: Big Read: East Africa renewed its brand for another ten years. The visa that would make it one destination is still a study.
item.description: EAC tourism ministers adopted a ten-year marketing strategy in Arusha last Thursday under a slogan the region already had. The single tourist visa that would let an operator actually sell the region got two more deadlines and no decision.

item.title: Big Read: The breach happened at the software company. Under three East African laws, it is the hotel that has to report it.
item.description: A French hotel software publisher lost roughly 135GB of guest records from about 1,500 establishments between 27 September and 5 October, and the fraud calls began the next day carrying real booking references. item.title: Big Read: The Gulf added a third daily flight to Nairobi while its own hub was losing a third of its passengers. That is not confidence, it is surplus.
item.description: Dubai International carried 31% fewer passengers in the first half of 2026 and Middle East arrivals fell 22%, yet Emirates put a third daily service into Nairobi on 1 July and signed a marketing agreement with the Kenya Tourism Board in September. item.title: Big Read: The most movable money in travel is shopping for a destination. Kenya has been bidding with a building site.
item.description: Nine in ten meeting planners expect to spend more in 2027 and four in ten have already moved an event's destination under cost and geopolitical pressure. Africa holds about 4% of the world's association meetings, and the two East African capitals chasing the segment this week are chasing two very different versions of it.

item.title: Big Read: Kenya is about to re-grade its hotels. The stars being sold today were set in 2018.
item.description: The Tourism Regulatory Authority starts its national classification exercise in Nairobi and Kiambu on 26 October, eight years after the last one. Kenya is the only EAC state with more four-star hotels than three-star, and its public register of classified hotels currently returns a single record named Test Entity 1.

item.title: Big Read: Zanzibar's taxman is moving into the booking system. The levy is not the expensive part.
item.description: Zanzibar's revenue authority published an amendment to its Virtual Fiscal Management System regulations on 1 September requiring accommodation providers to run an approved property management system wired into the state's platform. item.title: Big Read: Someone else is selling your lodge under your own name. The defences were built for other countries.
item.description: A report published on 9 October put 1.1 million brand-hijacking adverts against 204,000 hotels in 205 countries. East African properties are already on the pages those adverts lead to, and the three remedies working elsewhere are the three that travel worst.
